2026-11-18.q: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
opts: Hackers stole money from the accounts of 1.8 million credit union members.
A suspected breach at a software provider used by 43 credit unions may have exposed the personal data of many members, raising concerns about fraud.
The Data Protection Commission has fined Wellington IT for failing to protect member records.
Constellation Software has decided to sell Wellington IT following the incident.
2026-11-18.exp: The passage centres on "a suspected data breach involving 43 credit unions" that originated at Wellington IT and "could potentially" affect "approximately 1.8 million individuals", with phishing the main risk. No money was taken, as "accounts and balances remained uncompromised" (A); no fine is mentioned (C); and no sale is reported (D).

2026-11-18.q: What can be inferred about why so many credit unions were affected?
opts: Each credit union was attacked separately by different groups of hackers.
The credit unions had all ignored warnings from the Central Bank.
The breach happened inside the Department of Finance's own systems.
Many credit unions depend on the same external software platform, so one weakness affected them all.
2026-11-18.exp: The passage says the firm "supplies the banking platform for more than a third of Irish credit unions, which consequently magnifies the potential scale of the incident", implying that shared reliance on one provider spread the risk. Nothing suggests separate attacks (A), ignored warnings (B), or a breach at the Department (C).

2026-11-18.q: Why does the writer mention that the stolen records "contain authentic personal details"?
opts: To explain why phishing messages based on them could be especially convincing.
To show that the hackers failed to obtain any useful information.
To prove that account balances have been changed.
To suggest that members should close their credit union accounts.
2026-11-18.exp: The sentence continues: "fraudulent communications are likely to appear considerably more credible, thereby increasing the probability that recipients will disclose confidential information." The detail explains the phishing risk, not that the data was useless (B), that balances changed (C), or that accounts should be closed (D).

opts: Ireland has met its 2030 climate targets ahead of schedule.
Mary Robinson has been appointed to lead Ireland's delegation at Cop31.
Mary Robinson's criticism that Ireland's climate action is too slow, and the climate minister's defence of the Government's record.
The European Union has agreed to cancel Ireland's climate compliance payments.

2026-11-18-2.q: What can be inferred about the estimate of compliance payments of up to €26 billion?
opts: The minister does not accept that the cost will be as high as the advisers project.
The Government has already paid this amount to the European Union.
Mary Robinson produced the estimate herself.
The figure refers to the cost of the National Development Plan.

It is a future estimate, not a payment already made (B); it comes from "independent climate and fiscal advisers", not Robinson (C); and it concerns the emissions "shortfall", not the Development Plan (D).

2026-11-18-2.q: How would you describe O'Brien's response to Robinson's criticism?
opts: Dismissive and personally insulting towards her.
Fully in agreement that the Government's approach has failed.
Confused and unable to give any examples of progress.
Respectful of her, yet firm in defending the Government's overall approach.

He was neither insulting (A), fully in agreement (B), nor short of examples (C).

opts: RTÉ has announced it will stop commissioning independent productions.
Independent producers argue that a proposed €20 million cut to RTÉ's funding threatens their sector and call for stable, multi-annual funding.
Netflix and Disney have agreed to pay a new content levy in Ireland.

opts: To argue that the sector no longer needs public funding.
To criticise producers for spending too much money.
To show that the €20 million cut has already been reversed.
To stress the sector's economic importance and support the case for predictable funding.

opts: Public EV charging in Ireland has become more expensive while the charging network is failing to keep pace with rising demand.

Ireland has 95 chargers per 100,000 versus 820 in the Netherlands (B), prices rose (C), and EVs "have surpassed petrol, diesel and hybrid models" (D).

2026-11-18-4.q: What can be inferred about drivers who live in apartments?
opts: They usually pay less for charging than people with driveways.
They are exempt from ESB's price increases.
They are likely to feel the impact of higher public charging prices more than homeowners with a private charger.
They are prevented by law from owning electric vehicles.

So they bear the increase more heavily, not less (A); there is no exemption (B) or legal ban (D).

2026-11-18-4.q: What is the writer's attitude towards the Government's community charging hub strategy?
opts: Enthusiastic, presenting it as a complete solution.
Cautiously sceptical, noting a limitation that may reduce its usefulness.
Angry, demanding that the strategy be withdrawn.
Neutral, offering no evaluation of it at all.
